analysis.one_liner: Holds private equity firms financially responsible when companies they take over fail, and taxes their managers' profits like regular income.
analysis.headline: The bill spent its entire life in committee—referred to four House committees and then a subcommittee—and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules for private equity firms that buy companies. It would make the funds—and even their investors—liable for the debts and legal penalties of companies they control, block a company from paying big dividends to its buyout fund for two years after an acquisition, move unpaid wages, severance, and pension obligations to the front of the line in bankruptcy, and tax fund managers' 'carried interest' at ordinary income rates instead of lower capital-gains rates. It would also require funds to publicly disclose their fees and returns and restrict the packaging of risky corporate debt for investors.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies owned by private equity funds—nearly 5.8 million people when the bill was filed—would have first claim on unpaid wages, severance, and benefits in bankruptcy instead of standing behind lenders [S3]. Retail employees at chains like Sears, Toys "R" Us, and Payless, whose bankruptcies the bill cites, would benefit from rules that stop funds from extracting dividends before a collapse and void transfers made before one [S3]. People holding gift cards and customer deposits would recover up to $1,800 in priority [S3]. Investors, including pension funds, would get standardized public disclosure of fund fees and returns and fiduciary protections [S2][S3]. The federal government would collect more revenue from managers whose 'carried interest' would be taxed as ordinary income [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees at buyout-owned companies

how_it_helps.text: Private funds and their investors would be jointly and severally liable for a target company's debts, legal penalties, WARN Act violations, and pension withdrawal liabilities, so workers and pension funds could collect directly from the fund when a portfolio company fails [S2][S3].

A company taken over by a private fund could not pay dividends, buybacks, or similar distributions to the fund for two years, and transfers made to the fund before a bankruptcy could be voided for up to eight years, with a court's help for employees and creditors to claw the money back [S3].

In bankruptcy, unpaid wages and benefits would be prioritized up to $20,000 per employee (double the current cap), severance pay would be treated as earned at layoff, and courts would have to weigh job preservation when approving asset sales [S3].
Carried interest—the profit share fund managers receive—would be taxed as ordinary income instead of lower-rate capital gains, ending a tax advantage worth billions to the industry [S2][S3].

Private funds would have to publicly disclose fees and returns under SEC rules and could no longer require investors to waive fiduciary protections, and lenders would have to keep a stake in risky corporate debt they securitize [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity fund managers would pay higher taxes on carried interest, face a surtax on payments extracted from controlled companies, and lose their ability to deduct interest on heavily indebted buyouts [S3]. Funds and their investors—including pension funds that hold economic interests—would bear joint liability for portfolio companies' debts, penalties, and pension shortfalls [S3]. Buyout-dependent lenders and securitizers of leveraged loans would face risk-retention requirements and lose fee income on deals the rules discourage [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity funds and their investors

drawbacks.text: The joint-and-several-liability provision reaches 'holders of economic interests' in a controlling fund, which could sweep in passive investors—including public pension funds that are major private equity investors—making retirement funds legally responsible for portfolio companies' debts and pension shortfalls [S3].

Banning dividends for two years, imposing a surtax on payments from controlled companies, limiting interest deductions, and subjecting leveraged-loan securitizations to risk retention would raise the cost of buyouts; some acquisitions do restore viable companies, and the bill's own supporters concede success stories exist even as they argue the losses fall on workers when deals fail [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker-protection and tax provisions are substantial and directly aimed at practices that left employees and retirees unpaid when chains like Sears and Toys "R" Us went under. But the liability design is broad: by making even passive holders of fund interests jointly liable, it could impose real costs on pension funds and raise the price of the buyout capital the industry deploys. On balance the bill would shift risk sharply from workers and pension beneficiaries onto fund managers and investors, with the main honest objection being that its tools are blunt enough to catch investors who never directed a takeover.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to four House committees on day one, then to a Judiciary subcommittee, it never got a committee vote, a floor vote, or any further action, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan (D-WI) introduced the bill on July 18, 2019, joined by eight other Democratic representatives as original cosponsors [S1][S3].

The same day, the House referred it to four committees—Ways and Means, Financial Services, Judiciary, and Education and Labor—splitting it across jurisdictions where it would need multiple chairmen to act [S5].
On August 12, 2019, the Judiciary portion was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, where it stayed [S5].
Seventeen House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it [S4].
No committee or subcommittee ever held a vote, no hearing or markup appears in the action record, and the bill received no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity fund managers and the recipients of carried interest are better off: they face no liability for portfolio-company failures, face no two-year dividend ban, and continue to pay lower capital-gains rates on carried interest. Companies that lend to or securitize leveraged buyouts also keep their current rules.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat (18 members in all, out of 231 Democrats), no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-controlled House never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill strips away the core protections of the buyout model: funds could no longer be shielded from portfolio-company debts and pension liabilities, barred from two-year dividend extractions, and exposed to eight-year clawback in bankruptcy. Workers at the nearly 5.8 million jobs in fund-owned companies were the people those practices were costing.

Manager profit shares would be taxed as ordinary income rather than at lower capital-gains rates, plus a surtax on payments extracted from controlled companies. This is a direct, multibillion-dollar tax increase on the wealthiest fund managers, paid at ordinary workers' rates on their labor-based income.

industries.industry: Leveraged lenders and securitizers of corporate debt
industries.note: Risk-retention requirements would force lenders to keep skin in the game on packaged corporate debt, cutting fee income on the risky loans that fund buyouts. The bill cites regulators' concern that these lenders collect fees while passing risk to unwitting investors.

industries.industry: Pension funds and institutional investors in private equity
industries.note: They would gain standardized public disclosure of fees and returns and enforceable fiduciary obligations, which the bill says funds currently let investors waive. But the same bill makes holders of economic interests in controlling funds jointly liable for portfolio companies' debts, which could expose pension funds' private equity allocations to direct liability.
